source.note: Runtime facts were not recorded; the turn is assumed to have ended cleanly with nothing in flight.

messages.text: The Java issues form several distinct defect families: lexical field ownership for inverse scans, enum switch-label binding, inherited invocation attribution, and field lookup in mirrored, local, and anonymous owners. I’ve traced the test bodies and their originating commits; I’m recording per-test evidence and preserving the fail-closed controls alongside the positive cases.

`cargo fmt` caught one malformed import: the automated tag insertion landed inside a multiline `use` block in the 2010 test file. I’m moving that import to module scope, then I’ll rerun formatting and checkpoint the reviewed batch.

The reviewed batch through issue #2072 is formatted and the tags now distinguish the defect cases from the semantic-pack enhancement’s cross-process integration gates. I’m saving this batch as a lane checkpoint; the JavaScript import-specifier golden conversion remains a separate, incomplete change until its expected output is generated and checked.

The prior checkpoint covers issue regressions through #2072. I’m continuing with the next reviewed groups, keeping the issue provenance ledger aligned as I go, then I’ll finish the golden conversion and lane validation.

The next batch contains nine confirmed bug regressions across Rust re-export/type lookup and C preprocessor guard handling. I’ve tagged them with issue-specific hardwon metadata and recorded per-test reasons; workspace-wide formatting is still running, so I’m checking that it only changes the assigned lane before committing.

The new hardwon batch is committed and exported to the lane mbox. I’ve confirmed formatting left only the intended issue files changed; I’m continuing through the C/C++ parser and guard regressions next.

This batch covers the anonymous-class naming panic, C# binder and generic-arity regressions, inherited constructor usages, and Scala scope selection. I also removed two tests that added no distinct regression signal: one had no competing member, and the other duplicated the exact retained Scala query.

The import-specifier golden now passes in bless mode and records ten structured lookup outcomes, including resolved named/default/namespace imports, aliased exports, a type-only import, and two fail-closed cases. The first attempts exposed a wrong occurrence index and a missing definitions array for unresolved results; both are corrected and captured in the runner.
I’m reading that naming note now while the Rust golden build finishes, then I’ll apply any naming correction before blessing or recording results.

The golden-name note confirms the new `symbols/rust-inline-module-items` case has a unique area and a feature-specific name. I’m finishing its verification, then I’ll resume the issue-ordered audit and package the lane report.

The #1142 golden case compiles and is in its unblessed verification run. The ledger currently has no duplicate decisions; 979 issue-suite tests still lack a decision, so I’m continuing the ordered audit after committing this conversion.

The remaining cases from #2177 onward include several verified defect fixes, including the Scala extractor resolution bug in #2186 and the C++ inverse-resolution bugs through #2207. I’m tagging each regression against its specific failure and recording its individual keep rationale in the ledger.

I’ve finished and committed the #2210–#2238 hard-won tags, excluding the six #2219 cases because they share one product-surface behavior family that is better represented as a golden. The ledger remains duplicate-free, and the patch export is current.

The #2219 golden now has a dedicated `symbols/scala-backtick-dotted-names` area, verified unique against the main checkout’s golden areas. Its six earlier cases are recorded as one shared golden; I’m resolving the first run now before committing the replacement.

The audit has now covered another 49 individually reasoned regressions through #2299, including a second product-surface golden. I’m checking the older unresolved issue files next, then I’ll continue forward from #2300; the decisions ledger and patch export are being kept in sync after every commit.

The oldest missing files exposed several additional defect regressions and one feature-only PHP test, which I removed. I also corrected the ledger’s test kinds to follow the stricter definitions; next I’m consolidating the C/Scala summary-selector round-trip pair into a language-specific golden.
I’ll read the golden-name note, then resume the in-progress golden conversion and continue the issue audit under the brief’s rules.

The note requires language- or feature-specific golden area names. `summary-selector-round-trip` is unique in the main checkout; its blessed test run has finished, and I’m checking the rendered expectations before recording it.

The #2451 golden passes in both blessed and unblessed runs, and its conversion is committed with the ledger updated. I’m moving on to the next unreviewed issue families and checking each test’s issue provenance before deciding whether to tag, keep, consolidate, or delete it.

The next batch is classified and recorded: defect regressions in #2409, #2413, #2419, #2430, and #2483–2485 are tagged `hardwon`; the five #2414 tier-count tests are retained as tricky complexity invariants. Repository-wide formatting is still running before I compile and run the changed tests.

The tagged regressions and retained tier-count tests all passed in the targeted run (18 passed; the scheduled-only #2485 case was skipped under the default cfg). I’ve recorded the next issue batch too, including #2505’s policy integration and incremental-rebuild invariants, and am validating those metadata changes now.

The latest 36-test batch passed, and I checkpointed the audit through #2557; the mbox export is current. The next issues split into true defects and feature additions, so I’m checking issue labels and test bodies before deciding which examples are hard-won or disposable.

This batch ties the audit decisions to the commits: Go/C# regressions, external JVM dispatch, the CLI subject-scan fix, and module-level summary binding are marked hard-won. The Python callable-metadata test stays as a tricky binding-contract test because it checks decorator and declaration-shape distinctions added by an enhancement.

The next remaining issues include service reuse, cache invalidation, alias identity, and C++ call typing. I’m checking which are actual defect fixes versus feature support so only defect regressions receive `hardwon` metadata.
I’ll read the golden-name note, then continue the active issue-test audit under its naming constraint.

The note requires golden area names to be unique and feature-specific. The existing area, `symbols/summary-selector-round-trip`, meets that; this next audit batch adds no golden area. I’m continuing with the already-reviewed issue tests and will record individual decisions in the lane ledger.
The shell has `python3` rather than `python`; the attempted edit script did not run. I’m rerunning it with the available interpreter, then I’ll validate the focused tests and lint.

I added issue-specific `hardwon` metadata to the defect regressions and recorded the two #2772 keeps separately: one covers ordering between the reference scan and scoring surface, the other checks cancellation and retry behavior. I’m running the focused issue tests now.
The focused run passed all 47 selected tests, including both #2772 keeps and the 45 tagged regressions. I’m moving on to the lane’s required workspace formatting and `suite_issues` clippy check.
The focused tests are green. Formatting completed cleanly; clippy is still compiling the root test target and its all-features dependencies, with no diagnostics so far.

Clippy has advanced through the language crates and is now checking the flow crate; it remains diagnostic-free. Once it finishes, I’ll review the recorded ledger and commit/export the lane checkpoint.
Clippy has reached the root package. The mbx cache emitted a warning about a removed issue-suite source file; compilation is continuing, so I’m checking whether that stale prediction is non-fatal.

This checkpoint is committed and exported as `3d3e07402d`; the focused tests and clippy passed. The ledger shows more issue-suite tests remain, so I’m identifying the next unreviewed files and continuing the audit rather than treating this batch as the full lane.

The next group is mainly defect regressions from the C differential work, plus older procedure-summary and conditional-include fixes. I also found one provenance false positive: `uses_fixture_limit` is a function embedded inside Rust source text used by another test, not a test harness entry; I’ll record it as fixture coverage so it doesn’t get mistaken for a removable test.

All 46 tests in this group passed. The #2964 merge/provenance and #2967 replay-invalidation cases are retained as tricky checks with independent state comparisons; the 46 defect tests are tagged with their specific issue provenance. I’m checkpointing this batch now.

Issue #3105 is an enhancement with a compact family of target-typed C# initializer examples, so I’m checking whether one golden case can preserve the useful behavior through navigation output and remove the duplicate feature tests. I’ll use a language-specific area and verify its name against the main checkout first.

The C# feature family now has one `suite_usages` golden runner under the unique area `csharp-target-typed-call-initializers`, with fixtures for overload ambiguity, named arguments, nested and shadowed scopes, static receivers, and partial types. I’m formatting and blessing the output next, then I’ll inspect every expected row before recording the conversion.

The first golden render exposed a mismatch in my verification path: `scan_usages_by_reference` returned zero or unproven hits for properties that the original tests check via an exact declaration target. I’m switching the golden scan rows to the product’s `scan_usages_by_location` interface with the property path, column, and FQN selector, matching the intended definition selection.

The exact-location scan fixed the nested, static, and partial-type cases, but it still reports `verified_absent` for the cross-file overload cases even though the original usage-graph tests expect proven hits. I’m aligning the fixture’s analyzer configuration with those original tests before deciding whether this is a real gap that must keep the tests.

The mismatch persists with the same explicit C# analyzer configuration as the source tests: the product usage tool reports `verified_absent` for `Interop.Options.Text` and `ZIndex`, while the original strategy asserts those exact call sites are proven. Per the plan, I’m abandoning this golden conversion, restoring the original tests, and recording the surface discrepancy for the parent instead of blessing it.
I’ll read the golden-names note now, then continue the assigned issue-test audit under its naming constraint.

The note confirms golden areas must be unique and feature-specific. The abandoned #3105 scan experiment left no golden artifacts; I’m continuing with the remaining issue-test decisions and will preserve that finding for the parent.

I found 515 provenance rows still undecided, beginning with two C receiver regressions before #3020. I’ve now recorded those, tagged the already-reviewed bug fixes, removed the internal-only #3064 example family, and am proceeding in small commits with the cache and Go-index edge cases retained as tricky.

The golden-name note is accounted for: this batch created no new golden area. I kept four #3108 tests that cross the independently authored semantic-pack/source-JAR boundary, and removed internal-only unused-import examples plus the JSDoc certainty family; next I’m auditing the Python flow and persisted-cache regressions.

The next batch contains mostly confirmed bugs, which I’m tagging with per-test defect reasons. For enhancement tests, I’m retaining the TypeIs/TypeGuard polarity, uncertainty, keyword-binding and wire-format cases because they exercise distinct soundness or schema boundaries; the RQL set-equality and “may” verdict tests also cross their policy publication surface.
I’ll reread the golden naming note, then continue the assigned issue-test audit from the current lane state and report the finished work through the required handback.

The note confirms that any golden area must be uniquely named and include its language or feature. This lane has no retained golden artifacts, so I’m moving on with the remaining 310 unreviewed tests and will judge each against its issue and source.

I’ve confirmed this first batch is mostly defect regressions. I tagged those tests, and kept the six #3284 cases because they exercise the RQL-to-policy boundary under ambiguity, incomplete evidence, and truncation. Next I’m checking the follow-on C++, C#, and Scala issue files for duplicates and feature-only examples.

The C++/C# and Scala batches are also defect pins, including negative controls that stop the fixes from widening resolution incorrectly. I’ve recorded their per-test reasons and am checkpointing these tags before continuing through the adapter and parser tests.

Formatting exposed a parse error in the lane’s earlier #3108 pruning: a dangling `#[ignore]` attribute is left at the end of that test file. It predates this batch but is within the lane’s owned suite, so I’m tracing and fixing that mechanical error before checkpointing.

The first checkpoint is in place. The audit found ten #3296 tags that were missing from the external decision ledger, so I’m reconciling that metadata while reviewing the configuration adapters—those need a closer boundary-by-boundary judgment because the issues add new formats rather than fix reported bugs.

The adapter tests are now reconciled: I kept the Java-properties reader’s external-format checks and removed only duplicated TOML cases and constant checks. The remaining Scala, C/C++, TypeScript, PHP, selector, and Python-root tests trace to fixes; I’m tagging them with the actual defect references, including follow-up commits.
I’ve read the golden-name note. I’m continuing the assigned audit with its naming constraint in force and will include the note’s effect in the handback report.

The note confirms there are no naming exceptions for this lane: I’ll avoid creating a new golden area unless a family truly needs conversion, and any area would have to be unique and language-specific. I found 83 tests still awaiting audit decisions; I’m checking their issue provenance and individual assertions before recording the remaining outcomes.

The remaining audit is now recorded for every provenance row. I classified the C++ #3507/#3508 suites as hard-won because they correct false unresolved behavior even though the tracker labels them enhancements; #3535 is a feature addition, so I kept its distinct integration boundaries and removed one redundant positive case. I’m formatting and validating the completed suite now.

Clippy found one scope issue: the JSON RQL regression sits inside a nested module, so the `hardwon` macro import at the file root is not visible there. I’m adding a module-local import, then I’ll rerun the check and save its log in the report directory.

The next clippy pass reached the suite but found a stale helper in the already-pruned #3131 file: `solve` has no callers after that file’s example deletions. I’m removing this unused helper, then I’ll rerun formatting and clippy; the warning is within the lane’s owned test paths.

I checked the existing golden tree as the note requires and found that earlier lane commits placed new cases under the shared generic `symbols` and `usages` roots. I’m moving those cases into four unique feature-specific areas and updating their runners before validation, so the lane no longer shares a golden area with another lane.

The renamed symbol goldens all pass under their new roots. The import/navigation golden is still compiling and running; once it finishes, I’ll finish the patch export and reconcile the handback counts, logs, and any open design findings.

after.text: All 1,617 provenance rows now have decisions, and the hard-won tags reconcile with the source. Final clippy passes; all four golden cases pass under unique feature-specific areas. I also removed the u
